# .github

Workflows, composite actions and repository settings, plus the moon setup CI runs through. Environments and stores they deploy into are in `infrastructure/AGENTS.md`.

## CI/CD, Branching, & Release Lifecycle

All build, test, infrastructure provisioning, and deployment pipelines run exclusively through GitHub Actions (bypassing GCP Cloud Build). Sequential execution rules ensure infrastructure provisioning completes successfully before service updates occur.

### Building with moon

[moon](https://moonrepo.dev/moon) **v2** is the CI build/lint/test orchestrator for the whole repo. `docs/architecture.md` has the history of how it got here and what was deliberately given up along the way; this section describes the system as it stands.

**The project map is a small, hand-written graph, not per-file inference.** `.moon/workspace.yml` maps every moon project: `services/*/moon.yml` and `packages/*/moon.yml` globs discover `services/backend`, `services/frontend` and `packages/protos` by folder (`projects.globFormat: 'source-path'`, so each project's ID is its own path rather than a short name); `root` (`.`), `infra-root` (`infrastructure/root`), `infra-env` (`infrastructure/env`) and `deploy-{root,staging,prod}` (`infrastructure/config/{root,staging,prod}`) are named explicitly, since none of them is glob-derived. Each project's own `moon.yml` declares `dependsOn` by hand - `services/backend` and `services/frontend` both depend on `packages/protos`; `deploy-staging`/`deploy-prod` depend on `infra-env` and `deploy-root` - rather than moon inferring an edge from an import or a Terraform reference. At this repo's size (about 8 projects, one Go module, one npm package, no cross-project imports to infer) there is nothing for import-level inference to find that a handful of declared edges doesn't already say more plainly, and `root`'s `projects-covered` task enforces the other half: it fails CI if a `services/*` or `packages/*` folder has no `moon.yml`, so a new project can't silently go undiscovered by the globs above.

**`--affected` is changed files only; a graph relation needs an explicit `inputs` entry.** moon v2's affected detection does not walk `dependsOn` by default - `-g`/`--include-relations` would, but nothing here uses it. Instead, a task that must react to a change outside its own project lists that project as an `inputs` entry directly (e.g. `services/backend:test` and `services/frontend:test` both list `project://packages/protos`, so a `.proto`-only edit still marks them affected without pulling in every other `packages/protos` dependent moon's own graph walk would reach). This is more typing per task than a transitive-dependents flag, and exactly as precise as the inputs actually declared. One input every task gets without declaring it: `.moon/tasks/all.yml`'s `implicitInputs` adds each project's own `moon.yml`, so a PR that edits a task's command also runs that task.

**The `deploy-{root,staging,prod}:plan` tasks are markers, not real Terraform runs.** Each is a `noop` command whose only job is its `inputs` list: `terraform.tfbackend`, `terraform.tfvars`, `project://infra-root` or `project://infra-env`, and every composite action/workflow file that environment's real plan/apply job depends on. `moon query affected`, run once per workflow in the `changed` job with `MOON_BASE` set to `origin/main` on a PR and to `github.event.before` on a push (the whole push, not just its last commit), checks whether each marker task shows up in the affected set - that's what decides whether `pull-request.yaml`'s `infrastructure-{root,staging,prod}` jobs (`terraform plan`) or `push-commit.yaml`'s (`terraform apply`) run. The marker's own `options.cache: false` and `runInCI` staying at its default (not `false`) both matter: a `runInCI: false`/`Skip` task is invisible to `moon query affected` in CI mode (moon's `AffectedTracker` excludes it outright), which would silently break every deployment decision - found the hard way when all three environments always read unaffected until that option was removed.

**`.github/actions/*` composite actions are per-deployment `inputs`, not a blanket glob.** Each `deploy-*:plan` marker's `inputs` names the exact composite actions and workflow files its own environment's job depends on (`terraform-pull-request`, `terraform-push-commit`, and for `deploy-root` alone, `gcp-secret-manager`), so a change to an action only staging's job uses does not mark prod affected too, with no repo-wide fallback glob to keep in sync alongside it.

**No GitHub Actions remote cache.** moon's remote cache only speaks the Bazel Remote Execution v2 API - there is no GHA backend for it - so this repo runs without one: `moon ci` already skips every unaffected project's tasks entirely, which is most of what a remote cache would buy here anyway. Revisit (e.g. a self-hosted `bazel-remote` on a GCS bucket) only if CI time becomes a real problem.

**`moon ci`'s target list is split one-for-one with the required jobs**: `lint-check` runs `moon ci :format :lint :vet :typecheck :build :validate root:wire-types root:projects-covered root:go-version-sync`, `test` runs `moon ci :test services/backend:image`, and `protos-drift` runs `moon ci packages/protos:drift` - each against `MOON_BASE: origin/main`. The leading `:` on a target (`:format`, `:test`, ...) is moon's "run this task in every project that has it" syntax; a project without a given task is silently skipped, not an error, which is what makes `services/backend:test services/frontend:test packages/protos:lint ...` collapse into one `:test`/`:lint` per job. `services/backend:image` (the Docker build discussed in `services/backend/AGENTS.md`) rides the same `test` job, for the same reason `test` covers anything else that must pass before merge: a broken image build fails the PR that causes it rather than surfacing first on the merge job that publishes it. The frontend bundle (`services/frontend:build`, `npm run build`) builds the same way, since moon runs every task in the real checkout with no sandbox to hide a build input from.

**`.prototools` (repository root) is the single source of every pinned tool version** - `moon`, `go`, `node`, `npm`, `buf`, `terraform` - read by [proto](https://moonrepo.dev/proto) both in CI (`moonrepo/setup-toolchain`) and locally (`proto install`), so a version lives in exactly one file rather than also inside `bufbuild/buf-setup-action`'s `version:` input or a workflow's own `setup-go`/`setup-node` step. The `buf` and `terraform` entries are third-party proto plugins (proto's `registry/data/third-party.json`), pinned to a commit SHA rather than a branch: both verify a checksum on download, so this pins what they're *fetched from*, not what's trusted on top of that.

Terraform's own project graph is modeled the same hand-written way moon models everything else: `infrastructure/env` and `infrastructure/root` are `infra-env`/`infra-root` projects with no tasks of their own beyond the `format` (`terraform fmt -check`) and `validate` (`terraform init -backend=false && terraform validate`, `runInCI: 'only'`) both inherit from `.moon/tasks/terraform.yml`, and each of `infrastructure/config/{staging,prod,root}` is a `deploy-*` project whose `plan` marker task is described above. moon has no HCL parser of its own and runs every task in the host's own environment, unsandboxed, so `terraform init`'s provider installer sees the runner's real `PATH` without anything needing to declare it should.

### Versioning

Releases use plain semantic versioning — `major.minor.patch`, with no `-rc.N` or other pre-release suffix on the tag itself (pre-release vs. formal release is tracked via GitHub's release "prerelease" flag, not the tag name). The bump on every merge to `main` is calculated automatically from the Conventional Commit subjects landed since the last tag, via the [`trunk-based-release-versioning`](https://github.com/Fresa/trunk-based-release-versioning) action: a bare `feat:` bumps **minor**, a breaking change (`!` or `BREAKING CHANGE:`) bumps **major**, and everything else bumps **patch**, with major taking precedence over minor over patch when a range of commits mixes types. Developers can still rename the generated pre-release before promotion if the calculated bump isn't the one they want.

### Staging Deployments (Push to main)

Merging a pull request to `main` automatically builds the backend container image and pushes the same bytes, tagged with the commit SHA (never the calculated version — that can still change if a developer renames the pre-release before promotion), to **both** the `blog-gorman-club-stag` and `blog-gorman-club-prod` Artifact Registries - this runs on every merge regardless of whether `services/backend/**` changed, so every commit on `main`, and therefore every release tag, has an image under its SHA in both registries. It is then deployed to Cloud Run in the `blog-gorman-club-stag` project alone and the staging subdomain on Cloudflare Pages is updated; the prod push has nothing deployed against it yet, since staging is where the commit is validated first. The frontend is built the same way and on the same schedule — every merge, whether or not `services/frontend/**` changed — as a plain `dist/` (`frontend-build`), with no backend URL baked in: the bundle carries nothing environment-specific, so the identical bytes are uploaded under a `<commit-sha>/` folder into **both** the `blog-gorman-club-stag-frontend` and `blog-gorman-club-prod-frontend` buckets (`frontend-publish`). The staging site is then deployed straight from that same `dist/`, so nothing is rebuilt separately for the live staging site; the prod bucket's folder has nothing deployed against it yet, same as the prod registry.

### Pre-Release Generation

Merges to `main` calculate the next version (see Versioning above), summarize commit messages since the last tag, execute a `terraform plan -lock=false` against the production environment, and auto-generate a GitHub Pre-Release. This entry includes the plan output and the commit summary. The plan is read-only and disables state locking so it never contends with an in-flight production `terraform apply`, and so a pre-release build on `main` can never block a promotion from applying. Multiple pre-releases can accumulate on `main` without touching production.

The version number itself is calculated by its own `version` job, separate from `pre-release` and gated on nothing - unlike actually cutting the tag/release (below), computing the number is read-only, so there's no invariant it could break by running before the publish jobs finish. This is what lets `services-frontend` write the exact tag this commit is about to become into `config.json` (see Staging Deployments above and `services/frontend/README.md`), so the account panel can link to a real GitHub release instead of showing a raw commit SHA that says nothing about it. `pre-release` still recomputes the same calculation locally, but only for `last-version` and the commit log its release notes are built from - a job output is a string, not the file that calculation also writes - and takes the tag itself from the `version` job's output rather than its own recompute, so the tag staging already displays and the tag actually cut can never disagree.

`pre-release` itself stays unconditional on the diff - the same "runs every merge" invariant Staging Deployments (above) describes for `services-backend`/`services-frontend` - but it does wait on those two jobs having published and on `version` having computed the number, via `needs: [services-backend, services-frontend, version]` plus an explicit `if:` of its own. Without that, a tag could be cut for a commit those publish jobs never built, breaking the "every release tag has a commit-SHA image/folder in both environments" invariant in the one way promotion can't recover from - there's nothing to deploy and nothing to roll back to.

### Production Releases (Manual Promotion)

Promoting a specific pre-release tag via GitHub Actions converts it into a formal Release (e.g., `v1.0.0`) and runs, in order:

1. `terraform apply` on `blog-gorman-club-prod`, applying any infrastructure changes first.
2. Backend deploy: `gcloud run deploy` in `blog-gorman-club-prod`, pointed at `<region>-docker.pkg.dev/blog-gorman-club-prod/backend/backend:${{ github.sha }}` - the workflow resolves the target commit SHA directly from the release tag pointer (`github.sha`), and that tag is already sitting in prod's own registry, pushed there when this commit was built and deployed to staging (see Staging Deployments above). There is no registry copy and no retag: the commit SHA is the only tag an image ever carries - the release-tag-to-SHA mapping already lives in GitHub - so promotion is nothing more than deploying an image already in place. Images are **never rebuilt** for production; prod runs the identical bytes validated in staging because they are the identical bytes, not a copy of them.
3. Frontend deploy: the commit-SHA folder already sitting in the `blog-gorman-club-prod-frontend` bucket, pushed there when this commit was built and deployed to staging (see Staging Deployments above), is downloaded (`frontend-fetch`) and deployed to the production subdomain on Cloudflare Pages, with `config.json` written next to it from the just-promoted backend URL — the one step with no backend analogue, since a static site has no runtime environment of its own to read a URL from. There is no cross-project read and no copy: the bucket promotion reads from is prod's own, and the bundle is never rebuilt, since the backend URL is runtime configuration rather than baked into it (see `services/frontend/src/lib/config.ts`).

Because staging applies on every merge but prod only applies here, prod's Terraform state can lag `main` by however long it takes someone to promote - ordinarily harmless, since nothing reads a resource before it exists, but a merge-time job that unconditionally *writes* into every environment's store (per Artifact Stores in `infrastructure/AGENTS.md`) has nothing to write into if the target resource is new and prod hasn't been promoted past the PR that added it. `apply-infrastructure-prod.yaml` (**Apply Prod Infrastructure (Manual)**, `workflow_dispatch` only) exists solely to close that gap: it runs step 1 above - `terraform apply` on `blog-gorman-club-prod` - on its own, with no release attached, so a newly-added per-environment resource can be backfilled into prod immediately after its PR merges, ahead of whenever the next promotion would otherwise get around to it. It requires typing `apply` into a confirmation input and shares Promote Release's concurrency group, since both mutate the same prod state. **This is not the normal path.** Prod infrastructure is meant to change through an actual promotion, where the accumulated plan was already visible in a pre-release's notes before anyone applied it; reach for this workflow only to bootstrap a specific new resource a merge is about to depend on, not as a routine way to push infra changes to prod.

### Rollback Strategy

Promoting a previous release tag re-runs the same promotion flow: `terraform apply` using that release's infrastructure configuration, then deploying Cloud Run in `blog-gorman-club-prod` straight to that release's own commit-SHA image tag - already sitting in prod's registry since the commit was built, so the deploy is harmless to repeat. The frontend's rollback is the same flow applied to its own bucket folder: that release's commit-SHA folder is re-fetched from `blog-gorman-club-prod-frontend` (already sitting there, so the fetch is harmless to repeat) and redeployed to Cloudflare Pages with that release's own `config.json` written beside it - no rebuild, for either service, ever.

### Pipeline Safety & Reusability

- **Concurrency Controls** — Every pipeline enforces an environment-scoped concurrency group to prevent overlapping commits from executing concurrent `terraform apply` steps or corrupting state locks.
- **Composite Actions** — Common pipeline steps (such as running Terraform plans/applies or building and pushing Docker images) are extracted into local GitHub Composite Actions inside `/.github/actions/` to keep root workflow files DRY and maintainable.
